chapter.name: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
chapter.blurb: The chapter goes beyond the single particle to extended bodies: it defines the centre of mass of a system of particles, shows that it moves as if all the external forces acted on the whole mass placed there, and introduces the vector product. It then builds rotational motion about a fixed axis in parallel with linear motion: angular velocity and acceleration, torque, angular momentum, moment of inertia, and the equation tau = I alpha. It also covers the equilibrium of rigid bodies with the principle of moments and the centre of gravity, and the conservation of angular momentum.

scope_in.item: State what a rigid body is and classify its motion as pure translation, rotation about a fixed axis, rotation with one point fixed (top, oscillating fan) or a combination of translation and rotation (rolling described qualitatively)
Locate the centre of mass of two, three and n particles from X = (sum of m_i x_i)/M and its y, z and vector forms; use the property that the sum of m_i r_i is zero about the centre of mass

Use symmetry to place the centre of mass of homogeneous rods, rings, discs, spheres, cylinders and cubes at the geometric centre, of a triangular lamina at the centroid, and find it for an L-shaped lamina or a disc with a hole by replacing pieces with point masses (Examples 6.1-6.3, Exercises 6.1, 6.2, 6.15)
Use M A = F_ext: the centre of mass moves as if all mass and all external forces were concentrated there; internal forces cancel by Newton's third law (exploding projectile)

Use P = M V and dP/dt = F_ext; apply conservation of total linear momentum and constancy of the centre-of-mass velocity when the external force is zero (radioactive decay, binary stars, child on a trolley)

Define the vector product: magnitude ab sin(theta), direction by the right-handed screw / right-hand rule; use its properties (non-commutative, distributive, a x a = 0, behaviour under reflection), the unit-vector products and the determinant form (Example 6.4, Exercise 6.4)

Use angular velocity as common to all particles of a body rotating about a fixed axis, v = omega r and v = omega x r, the direction of omega along the axis, and angular acceleration alpha = d(omega)/dt
Apply the kinematic equations of rotation with uniform angular acceleration, including conversion between rev/min and rad/s (Examples 6.10, 6.11)

Compute torque tau = r x F and angular momentum l = r x p of a particle (magnitudes via perpendicular distance, directions via the right-hand rule), use dl/dt = tau, and state when each is zero (Examples 6.5, 6.6, Exercises 6.6, 6.7)
For a system of particles use dL/dt = tau_ext, explain why internal torques cancel, and state the conservation of total angular momentum when the external torque is zero
State and apply the two conditions of mechanical equilibrium, recognise partial equilibrium and couples, and show that the moment of a couple is independent of the origin (Example 6.7)

Apply the principle of moments to levers (load arm x load = effort arm x effort, mechanical advantage) and to bars, metre sticks, cars and ladders in equilibrium with weight acting at the centre of gravity (Examples 6.8, 6.9, Exercises 6.9, 6.16)
Define the centre of gravity as the point of zero total gravitational torque, relate it to the centre of mass, and describe finding it by balancing or by suspension

Define moment of inertia I = sum of m_i r_i^2 through K = (1/2) I omega^2, recall and use the eight entries of Table 6.1, the radius of gyration (I = M k^2) and the purpose of a flywheel (Exercise 6.11)
Use dW = tau d(theta), P = tau omega and tau = I alpha for rotation about a fixed axis, including a cord wound on a wheel or cylinder (Example 6.12, Exercises 6.10, 6.13, 6.14)
Use L = I omega for a body rotating about a fixed axis of symmetry and the conservation of I omega when no external torque acts (swivel chair, acrobat, diver, turntable; Exercise 6.12)

concepts.name: Rigid bodies and the kinds of motion they can have
concepts.description: The idea of a rigid body, pure translation, rotation about a fixed axis, rotation with only one point fixed, and motion that combines translation with rotation.
concepts.idea: A rigid body keeps the distance between every pair of its particles fixed, and its motion is pure translation, rotation, or a combination of the two.
concepts.rule: Ideally a rigid body has a perfectly definite and unchanging shape; no real body is truly rigid, but the deformations are often negligible. In pure translation all particles have the same velocity at any instant. A body fixed along a straight line can only rotate about that line (the axis of rotation): every particle moves in a circle that lies in a plane perpendicular to the axis and has its centre on the axis, and particles on the axis stay at rest. In more general rotation (a spinning top, an oscillating table fan) only one point is fixed; the axis passes through that point but is not fixed, and the movement of a top's axis around the vertical is called precession. A body that is not pivoted or fixed has either pure translation or a combination of translation and rotation (a cylinder rolling down an incline); a body pivoted or fixed in some way has rotation. This chapter treats rotation about a fixed axis only.
concepts.example: A potter's wheel and a merry-go-round rotate about a fixed axis; a box pushed across a floor without turning is in pure translation.

concepts.name: Centre of mass of a system of particles and of a rigid body
concepts.description: Locating the centre of mass of two, three and many particles from the mass-weighted mean of their positions, and of homogeneous bodies and laminas by symmetry.
concepts.idea: The centre of mass is the mass-weighted mean position of all the particles of a system.
concepts.rule: For two particles on the x-axis X = (m1 x1 + m2 x2)/(m1 + m2); for equal masses the centre of mass is midway between them. For n particles X = (sum of m_i x_i)/M, Y = (sum of m_i y_i)/M, Z = (sum of m_i z_i)/M with M the total mass; in vector form R = (sum of m_i r_i)/M. For three particles of equal mass it is the centroid of the triangle they form. With the origin at the centre of mass, the sum of m_i r_i is zero. A rigid body is treated as a continuous distribution: X = (1/M) integral of x dm, and so on. For homogeneous bodies of regular shape (thin rod, ring, disc, sphere, cylinder, cube) reflection symmetry places the centre of mass at the geometric centre; for a uniform triangular lamina it is the centroid, where the medians meet. A lamina made of simple pieces is handled by replacing each piece with a point mass at its own centre of mass.
concepts.example: Particles of 1 kg at x = 0 and 4 kg at x = 5 m: X = (1 x 0 + 4 x 5)/(1 + 4) = 4 m, nearer the heavier particle.

questions.q: From a uniform circular disc of radius 12 cm, a circular hole of radius 6 cm is cut out. The centre of the hole is 6 cm from the centre O of the original disc. Locate the centre of mass of the remaining body.
questions.a: Take O as origin and the x-axis through the centre of the hole. Mass is proportional to area, so if the full disc has mass M, the removed piece has mass M/4 (its radius is half) and the remaining body 3M/4. The full disc is the remaining body plus the removed piece, and its centre of mass is at O: 0 = [(3M/4) x + (M/4)(6 cm)]/M. Hence x = -2 cm. The centre of mass of the remaining body is 2 cm from O, on the side opposite to the hole.
s: Removed mass is M/4 and remaining mass 3M/4 (mass proportional to area)
Full disc = remaining body + removed piece, with centre of mass at O: (3M/4) x + (M/4)(6 cm) = 0
x = -2 cm: 2 cm from O on the side opposite the hole

questions.q: To find the centre of mass of a uniform triangular lamina LMN, a student divides it into narrow strips parallel to the base MN and argues that the centre of mass lies on the median from L. Is the argument sound, and is it enough to fix the point?
questions.a: The argument is sound: each narrow strip has its centre of mass at its mid-point by symmetry, and the mid-points of all the strips lie on the median from L, so the centre of mass of the whole lamina lies on that median. It is not enough to fix the point; repeating the argument with strips parallel to another side shows it also lies on a second median, so it is at their point of intersection, the centroid.
s: Sound - mid-points of the strips all lie on the median from L
Not sufficient alone - a second median is needed; the intersection (centroid) is the centre of mass

concepts.name: Motion of the centre of mass and linear momentum of a system
concepts.description: The equation of motion of the centre of mass, the total linear momentum of a system of particles and its conservation when the total external force is zero.
concepts.idea: The centre of mass moves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all the external forces acted there; internal forces cannot change its motion.
concepts.rule: Differentiating M R = sum of m_i r_i gives M V = sum of m_i v_i and M A = sum of m_i a_i = F1 + F2 + ... . Internal forces occur in equal and opposite pairs (Newton's third law) and cancel, so M A = F_ext. The total linear momentum is P = sum of m_i v_i = M V, and dP/dt = F_ext. If the total external force is zero, P is constant and the centre of mass moves with constant velocity, though individual particles may follow complicated paths. Illustrations: the centre of mass of the fragments of an exploding projectile continues on the same parabola; the products of the decay of a radium nucleus move so that their centre of mass keeps moving as the nucleus did, and back to back in the frame where the centre of mass is at rest; the two stars of a binary circle their centre of mass while it moves uniformly in a straight line.

concepts.name: Vector product of two vectors
concepts.description: Definition of the vector (cross) product, the right-hand rule for its direction, its properties, the products of the unit vectors and the component (determinant) form.
concepts.idea: The vector product a x b is a vector of magnitude ab sin(theta), perpendicular to the plane of a and b, with its sense fixed by the right-hand rule.
concepts.rule: c = a x b has magnitude ab sin(theta), where theta is the smaller angle (less than 180 degrees) between a and b; c is perpendicular to the plane containing a and b, in the direction a right-handed screw advances when turned from a to b (or the stretched thumb of the right hand when the fingers curl from a to b). It is not commutative: a x b = -(b x a). It does not change sign under reflection. It is distributive over addition: a x (b + c) = a x b + a x c. a x a = 0 (the null vector). For the unit vectors of a right-handed system: i x i = j x j = k x k = 0; i x j = k, j x k = i, k x i = j; j x i = -k, k x j = -i, i x k = -j (cyclic order positive). In components a x b = (a_y b_z - a_z b_y) i + (a_z b_x - a_x b_z) j + (a_x b_y - a_y b_x) k, which is the determinant with rows (i, j, k), (a_x, a_y, a_z), (b_x, b_y, b_z).
concepts.example: With i x j = k: for a = i + j and b = i - j, a x b = (a_x b_y - a_y b_x) k = (1 x (-1) - 1 x 1) k = -2k.

concepts.name: Angular velocity, angular acceleration and kinematics of rotation about a fixed axis
concepts.description: Angular velocity of a rotating rigid body and its relation v = omega x r with linear velocity, angular acceleration, and the kinematic equations for uniform angular acceleration.
concepts.idea: Every particle of a body rotating about a fixed axis has the same angular velocity omega, and its linear speed is omega times its perpendicular distance from the axis.
concepts.rule: omega = d(theta)/dt is the same for all particles and is the angular velocity of the whole body; v = omega r for a particle at perpendicular distance r from the axis, so particles on the axis are at rest. Angular velocity is a vector along the axis, in the direction a right-handed screw advances when its head is turned with the body; reversing the sense of rotation reverses it. In vector form v = omega x r, with r measured from an origin on the axis. Angular acceleration alpha = d(omega)/dt; for a fixed axis the direction of omega is fixed and only its magnitude may change. For uniform angular acceleration: omega = omega0 + alpha t; theta = theta0 + omega0 t + (1/2) alpha t^2; omega^2 = omega0^2 + 2 alpha (theta - theta0). One revolution is 2 pi rad, so n rev/min = 2 pi n/60 rad/s.
concepts.example: A wheel starting from rest with uniform alpha = 2 rad/s^2: after 5 s, omega = 2 x 5 = 10 rad/s and theta = (1/2) x 2 x 5^2 = 25 rad.

concepts.idea: Torque tau = r x F is the rotational analogue of force and angular momentum l = r x p the analogue of linear momentum; torque is the rate of change of angular momentum.
concepts.rule: Moment of force (torque) about the origin: tau = r x F, of magnitude rF sin(theta) = r_perp F = r F_perp, where r_perp is the perpendicular distance of the line of action from the origin; dimensions M L^2 T^-2 (same as work, but torque is a vector), SI unit N m. Torque is zero if r = 0, F = 0 or the line of action passes through the origin. Angular momentum of a particle: l = r x p (the moment of momentum), magnitude rp sin(theta) = r_perp p; it is zero if p = 0, r = 0 or the line of p passes through the origin. dl/dt = tau, the rotational analogue of F = dp/dt. For a system L = sum of r_i x p_i and dL/dt = tau_ext: internal torques cancel, assuming Newton's third law and that the forces between two particles act along the line joining them. If the total external torque is zero, L is constant, i.e. Lx, Ly and Lz are each constant.
concepts.example: With i x j = k: a force F = 2j N acting at r = 3i m has torque tau = r x F = 6 (i x j) = 6k N m about the origin.

concepts.name: Equilibrium of a rigid body: couples, moments and centre of gravity
concepts.description: The two conditions of mechanical equilibrium, partial equilibrium, couples, the principle of moments for a lever, and the centre of gravity, applied to bars on supports and a ladder against a wall.
concepts.idea: A rigid body is in mechanical equilibrium only when the total external force and the total external torque on it are both zero.
concepts.rule: Translational equilibrium: the vector sum of the forces is zero. Rotational equilibrium: the vector sum of the torques is zero; if the body is in translational equilibrium this condition does not depend on the point about which torques are taken. For coplanar forces three conditions suffice: two for the force components and one for the torques. A body may be in partial equilibrium. A couple is a pair of equal and opposite forces with different lines of action; it produces rotation without translation and its moment is the same about every point. Principle of moments for a lever: load arm x load = effort arm x effort (d1 F1 = d2 F2); mechanical advantage = F1/F2 = d2/d1. The reaction at the fulcrum has no moment about the fulcrum. Anticlockwise moments are taken positive. The centre of gravity is the point about which the total gravitational torque is zero; it coincides with the centre of mass when g is the same over the body. The weight of a body acts at its centre of gravity; a suspended body hangs with its centre of gravity vertically below the point of suspension.
concepts.example: A load of 400 N placed 0.5 m from the fulcrum of a light lever is balanced by an effort of 100 N applied 2 m from the fulcrum, since 0.5 x 400 = 2 x 100; the mechanical advantage is 4.

concepts.name: Moment of inertia, radius of gyration and rotational kinetic energy
concepts.description: The definition of moment of inertia from the kinetic energy of rotation, its values for the standard bodies of Table 6.1, the radius of gyration and the role of a flywheel.
concepts.idea: Moment of inertia I = sum of m_i r_i^2 is the rotational analogue of mass; it depends on how the mass is distributed about the chosen axis.
concepts.rule: A body rotating about a fixed axis with angular velocity omega has kinetic energy K = (1/2) I omega^2, where I = sum of m_i r_i^2 and r_i is the perpendicular distance of the i-th particle from the axis. I does not depend on omega; it depends on the mass, shape and size of the body, the distribution of mass about the axis and the position and orientation of the axis. Dimensions M L^2, SI unit kg m^2. Table 6.1: thin ring about the axis through its centre perpendicular to its plane, M R^2; thin ring about a diameter, M R^2/2; thin rod about the perpendicular axis through its mid-point, M L^2/12; circular disc about the axis through its centre perpendicular to its plane, M R^2/2; disc about a diameter, M R^2/4; hollow cylinder about its axis, M R^2; solid cylinder about its axis, M R^2/2; solid sphere about a diameter, 2 M R^2/5. Two masses M/2 at the ends of a light rod of length l, about the perpendicular axis through the centre: M l^2/4. Radius of gyration k is defined by I = M k^2. A flywheel has a large moment of inertia and so resists sudden changes of speed.
concepts.example: A thin ring of mass 2 kg and radius 0.1 m, about the axis through its centre perpendicular to its plane: I = M R^2 = 2 x 0.01 = 0.02 kg m^2.

questions.q: A rigid body rotates about a fixed axis with angular velocity omega. Starting from the kinetic energy of one of its particles, derive the expression for the kinetic energy of the whole body in terms of omega.
questions.a: A particle of mass m_i at perpendicular distance r_i from the axis moves in a circle with speed v_i = r_i omega, so its kinetic energy is (1/2) m_i v_i^2 = (1/2) m_i r_i^2 omega^2. The total kinetic energy is the sum over all particles; omega is the same for every particle and can be taken out of the sum: K = (1/2) (sum of m_i r_i^2) omega^2. Defining I = sum of m_i r_i^2, K = (1/2) I omega^2. Comparing with (1/2) m v^2, I is the rotational analogue of mass.
s: Particle: v_i = r_i omega, kinetic energy (1/2) m_i r_i^2 omega^2
Sum over particles with omega common: K = (1/2)(sum of m_i r_i^2) omega^2
I = sum of m_i r_i^2 identified, giving K = (1/2) I omega^2

questions.q: A flywheel of mass 4 kg has a moment of inertia of 1 kg m^2 about its axle. A student writes its radius of gyration about the axle as k = I/M = 0.25 m. Evaluate this working.
questions.a: The working is wrong. The radius of gyration is defined by I = M k^2, so k^2 = I/M = 1/4 = 0.25 m^2 and k = 0.5 m. I/M is k^2, with unit m^2, not k; the student forgot to take the square root.
s: Uses I = M k^2: k^2 = I/M = 0.25 m^2
k = 0.5 m, not 0.25 m (square root omitted)

questions.q: You have two small masses of 0.5 kg each and a light rod. Design an arrangement, rotating about the axis through the mid-point of the rod and perpendicular to it, whose moment of inertia is 0.16 kg m^2. Then state how the same two masses should be repositioned to double the moment of inertia (sqrt(0.32) = 0.566).
questions.a: Fix the masses at equal distances d on either side of the axis: I = 0.5 d^2 + 0.5 d^2 = d^2. For I = 0.16 kg m^2, d = 0.4 m, i.e. the masses are at the ends of a light rod 0.8 m long. To double I to 0.32 kg m^2 without changing the masses, d^2 = 0.32, so each mass must be moved out to d = 0.566 m from the axis (a factor sqrt(2), not 2).
s: I = 2 x 0.5 x d^2 = d^2 for masses at distance d on either side of the axis
d = 0.4 m (rod 0.8 m long) for I = 0.16 kg m^2
Doubling I needs d = 0.566 m (distance increased by a factor sqrt(2))

concepts.name: Dynamics of rotation about a fixed axis and conservation of angular momentum
concepts.description: Work and power of a torque, tau = I alpha, the angular momentum L = I omega of a body rotating about a fixed axis of symmetry, and conservation of angular momentum when no external torque acts.
concepts.idea: For rotation about a fixed axis, torque produces angular acceleration (tau = I alpha), and when no external torque acts about the axis, I omega stays constant.
concepts.rule: Only forces lying in planes perpendicular to the axis, and only the components of position vectors perpendicular to the axis, contribute to the torque along the axis; components of torque perpendicular to the axis are cancelled by forces of constraint. Work done by a torque: dW = tau d(theta); power P = tau omega. For a rigid body the work done by the external torque goes into kinetic energy (1/2) I omega^2; equating rates gives tau = I alpha (I constant), Newton's second law for rotation about a fixed axis. Analogues: x and theta, v and omega, a and alpha, M and I, F and tau, p and L. The component of angular momentum along the axis is L_z = I omega; for a body symmetric about the axis L = I omega along the axis, but in general L and omega need not be parallel. d(I omega)/dt = tau; if the external torque about the axis is zero, I omega = constant, so a decrease in I (arms pulled in) increases omega, as on a swivel chair, for an acrobat, a diver or a dancer.
concepts.example: A torque of 10 N m acting on a wheel of moment of inertia 5 kg m^2 gives alpha = tau/I = 2 rad/s^2; at the instant its angular speed is 4 rad/s the torque delivers power P = tau omega = 40 W.

questions.q: A rope of negligible mass is wound round a hollow cylinder of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m, which is free to rotate about its own axis. The rope is pulled with a force of 20 N and does not slip. Find the angular acceleration of the cylinder and the linear acceleration of the rope.
questions.a: For a hollow cylinder about its axis I = M R^2 = 2 x 0.25 = 0.5 kg m^2. Torque tau = F R = 20 x 0.5 = 10 N m. alpha = tau/I = 10/0.5 = 20 rad/s^2. Since the rope does not slip, it moves with the speed v = R omega of the rim, so its linear acceleration is a = dv/dt = R alpha = 0.5 x 20 = 10 m/s^2.
s: I = M R^2 = 0.5 kg m^2 and tau = F R = 10 N m, giving alpha = 20 rad/s^2
a = R alpha = 10 m/s^2

Work done by the pull = 80 J
theta = 10 rad, omega^2 = 200, K = 80 J, equal to the work done

questions.q: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, derive tau = I alpha by equating the rate at which the external torque does work to the rate of increase of the kinetic energy of rotation. State the assumption made about I.
questions.a: The rate of doing work (power) is P = tau omega. The kinetic energy is (1/2) I omega^2; assuming I does not change with time (the mass is constant, the body stays rigid and the axis keeps its position in the body), d/dt[(1/2) I omega^2] = I omega (d omega/dt) = I omega alpha. For a rigid body there is no internal motion, so all the work goes into kinetic energy: tau omega = I omega alpha, hence tau = I alpha.
s: Rate of work = tau omega
Rate of increase of kinetic energy = I omega alpha, with I constant in time
Equating the two: tau = I alpha

questions.q: A student says: 'A rotor turning at a uniform angular speed has no angular acceleration, so the engine driving it at 200 rad/s supplies no torque and no power.' Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: It is true that uniform angular speed means zero net torque. But in practice a frictional torque opposes the rotation, so the engine must apply an equal torque to counter it. The engine therefore does deliver power P = tau omega, which is non-zero; only in the complete absence of friction would no torque be needed.
s: Uniform omega means zero NET torque, not zero applied torque
Engine torque balances the frictional torque, so power tau omega is delivered

questions.q: Compose a numerical problem about a child standing at the centre of a frictionless turntable who folds his outstretched arms, in which the angular speed rises from 30 rev/min to 75 rev/min. questions.a: One possible problem: 'A child stands at the centre of a turntable that rotates without friction at 30 rev/min, with his arms outstretched. He folds his arms, reducing the moment of inertia of the rotating system to 2/5 of its initial value. Find the new angular speed.' Solution: no external torque acts about the axis, so I1 omega1 = I2 omega2 and omega2 = (I1/I2) omega1 = (5/2) x 30 = 75 rev/min. Since K = (1/2) I omega^2, K2/K1 = (I2/I1) x (omega2/omega1)^2 = (2/5) x (2.5)^2 = 2.5. The kinetic energy becomes 2.5 times as large; the extra energy comes from the work the child does in pulling his arms in.
s: A complete problem in which the moment of inertia falls to 2/5 of its initial value (I1/I2 = 2.5)
I1 omega1 = I2 omega2 (no external torque) giving 75 rev/min
K2/K1 = (I2/I1)(omega2/omega1)^2 = 2.5
